title: Excessive disclosure of child browsing data to the AI recommendation engine
description: The planned flow sends child browsing data from the childprofiles collection to the AI recommendation engine. If the engine receives full browsing histories or unnecessary identifiers rather than only the minimum features needed for recommendation, this constitutes avoidable disclosure of children's personal data within the system.
assumptions: Assumes the recommendation function can operate on a reduced feature set, aggregated signals, or pseudonymized inputs instead of raw browsing data.

title: Inference of sensitive child traits from browsing history
description: Browsing data can allow the AI recommendation engine to infer sensitive attributes or highly intimate interests about a child, such as health concerns, vulnerabilities, developmental issues, religion, or other protected characteristics, beyond what was explicitly stored or expected for recommendation.
assumptions: Assumes the browsing data is sufficiently granular and the AI engine performs profiling or feature extraction that can derive latent attributes.
uncertainty_note: Exact subtree id is best-effort; applicability of inference is strong given AI processing of child browsing histories.

title: Secondary use of child browsing data for AI profiling beyond user expectations
description: Using child browsing data from profiles for AI recommendations may be incompatible with the original purpose for which the data was collected, especially if the planned use was not clearly communicated or expected by the child or guardian. This creates an unawareness risk around profiling and recommendation logic.
assumptions: Assumes the AI recommendation use is newly planned or not yet transparently disclosed in notices, consent flows, or parental controls.

title: Potential non-compliance from processing children's browsing data without a clear lawful basis and safeguards
description: Sending child browsing data to an AI recommendation engine may trigger heightened compliance obligations for children's data, profiling, transparency, purpose limitation, data minimization, and possibly parental authorization. If these safeguards are absent, the flow may violate applicable privacy requirements.
assumptions: Assumes the data concerns children and that the recommendation engine performs profiling or automated personalization.
uncertainty_note: Exact legal obligations depend on jurisdiction and implementation details; subtree id is best-effort.

title: Unnecessary disclosure of browsing data to third-party advertisers
description: The planned flow sends users' browsing data from the recommendation engine to third-party advertisers. This is an explicit disclosure of personal data across the system boundary and may violate data-minimization if the advertisers do not strictly need the full browsing data for the stated purpose.
assumptions: Browsing data is personal data or can reasonably be linked to an identifiable user or device; advertisers are separate third parties outside the system boundary.

title: Cross-context linkability via shared browsing profiles
description: Sharing browsing data with third-party advertisers can enable those advertisers to link a user's activity in this system with profiles, identifiers, or observations from other sites and services, increasing the ability to correlate records across contexts.
assumptions: Advertisers possess other identifiers, cookies, device fingerprints, or partner data that can be combined with the disclosed browsing data.

title: Identifiability of users from disclosed browsing data
description: Browsing histories, page visits, timestamps, and associated metadata may directly or indirectly identify individual users when transferred to advertisers, especially when combined with existing advertiser datasets.
assumptions: The browsing data includes persistent identifiers, quasi-identifiers, or sufficiently unique behavioral patterns.
uncertainty_note: Threat clearly applies in substance, but the exact tree-node id is approximate because the retrieved context does not include the detailed identifiability subtree.

title: Detectability of user activity by third-party advertisers
description: The existence, timing, and content of the outbound browsing-data flow may allow advertisers to detect that a particular user interacted with certain pages, products, or categories, even if full identity is not immediately known.
assumptions: The flow contains event timing, page/category information, or stable pseudonymous identifiers observable by the advertiser.
uncertainty_note: Detectability is a reasonable concern for this telemetry-sharing flow; exact subtree id is best judgement.

title: Sharing browsing data with advertisers without valid consent or compatible purpose
description: Sending browsing data to third-party advertisers may be non-compliant if users have not given valid, specific consent for advertising disclosure, or if the sharing exceeds the original purpose for which the data was collected.
assumptions: Applicable legal basis may require consent or strict purpose-compatibility for third-party advertising use of browsing data.
uncertainty_note: Non-compliance strongly depends on jurisdiction, legal basis, and notices/consent design; exact subtree id is approximate.

title: Excessive retention or storage of government ID images
description: Government ID images are highly sensitive personal data. Storing full images in the file-system backend may disclose more personal data than is strictly necessary for identity verification, especially if the full image is retained after verification or when extracted attributes would suffice.
assumptions: Assumes the system stores full ID images rather than immediately deleting them after verification or minimizing them to required attributes only.

title: Storage of ID images without adequate purpose limitation or legal basis
description: Persisting government ID images in backend/uploads may be non-compliant if the storage duration, purpose, or legal basis is not clearly defined and limited. This flow suggests collection and storage of special/highly sensitive identity evidence, which often requires strict necessity, transparency, and retention controls.
assumptions: Assumes the application is subject to privacy/data-protection obligations and that purpose limitation, retention, and lawful-basis requirements apply to stored identity documents.
uncertainty_note: Exact non-compliance node may differ depending on the LINDDUN Pro taxonomy version and applicable jurisdiction.

title: Stored ID images enable identification of the data subject
description: A government ID image directly identifies a person through name, photo, document number, address, date of birth, or other visible attributes. By storing these images in the file system, the datastore contains directly identifying records that can be tied to a specific individual.
assumptions: Assumes uploaded government ID images contain visible identifying fields, which is typical for such documents.
uncertainty_note: Identification is inherent to the data type; listed as a privacy threat because this flow creates a datastore of directly identifying artifacts.

title: Linkability across sessions or services via persistent ID document storage
description: Persistently storing government ID images can allow records from different sessions, accounts, or verification events to be linked to the same individual using stable identifiers present on the document (for example document number, name, face image, or date of birth).
assumptions: Assumes the stored files or associated metadata can be correlated across uploads, accounts, or processing events.
uncertainty_note: Applies if the system reuses or can correlate stored ID images or their metadata; if files are isolated and promptly deleted, this threat may be reduced.

title: JWT in localStorage enables cross-context linkability
description: Persisting a JWT in browser localStorage creates a stable client-side identifier/token that can be reused across sessions and browser contexts within the same origin. If multiple app features, scripts, or requests access and reuse the token, user actions can be linked together more easily than necessary.
assumptions: Assumes the JWT contains or functions as a stable identifier and is reused across requests or sessions.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-judgement because the retrieved context gives applicable threat types for Process→DataStore but not detailed node ids.

title: JWT contents may identify the user when stored client-side
description: A JWT often contains claims such as subject, email, tenant, roles, or other identifiers. Storing it in localStorage means any script executing in the origin can read those claims, making the user identifiable on the device/browser beyond what is strictly necessary for transient authentication.
assumptions: Assumes the JWT is not fully opaque and contains identifying claims, or can be trivially decoded to reveal them.
uncertainty_note: If the JWT is opaque and contains no identifying claims, identifiability impact is reduced.

title: localStorage persistence increases risk of unauthorized JWT disclosure
description: localStorage is readable by JavaScript in the origin and persists until explicitly cleared. If malicious or compromised scripts execute in the page, or if another local user/process can inspect browser storage, the JWT may be disclosed, exposing authentication state and any personal data embedded in the token.
assumptions: Assumes realistic risk of XSS, third-party script compromise, browser extension access, or local device compromise.
uncertainty_note: Node id is approximate; the threat itself is strong and well-established for browser localStorage token storage.

title: Users may be unaware that authentication tokens persist in localStorage
description: Storing the JWT in localStorage can create persistence beyond the user's expectation, especially on shared devices or after closing the browser. Users may not understand that their authenticated state or token remains stored locally and accessible until cleared or expired.
assumptions: Assumes the application does not clearly communicate token persistence behavior or provide intuitive controls to clear it.
uncertainty_note: Best-judgement node id; applicability depends on the application's transparency and UX.

title: Persistent client-side JWT storage may conflict with data minimization and storage limitation
description: Writing a JWT to localStorage may store more personal data than necessary on the client and retain it longer than needed for the authentication purpose. If the token includes user claims or long-lived session information, this can undermine privacy requirements such as minimization, storage limitation, and secure handling of authentication data.
assumptions: Assumes the JWT contains personal data or has a lifetime longer than strictly necessary.
uncertainty_note: Compliance impact depends on jurisdiction, token contents, retention period, and available alternatives such as HttpOnly secure cookies.

title: Parent can link child history across time into a detailed profile
description: The flow returns child history for review, which inherently aggregates multiple events over time. If the history includes recurring identifiers, timestamps, categories of activity, or contextual metadata, the parent can link separate records together to infer a richer profile of the child than any single record reveals.
assumptions: Assumes the returned history contains multiple records and stable identifiers or quasi-identifiers that enable correlation across sessions or events.

Even if explicit identifiers are minimized, the combination of attributes in the history may still identify the child.

If the full history is sent without filtering, summarization, or role-based minimization, the flow can disclose personal information beyond what is necessary for the parent's review purpose.

title: The child may be unaware that historical data is being shared for parental review
description: If the system does not clearly communicate to the child that their historical records are retrievable and shown to the parent, the flow can create a detectability issue: the child may not be able to detect when, what, or how much of their history has been accessed and shared.
assumptions: Assumes the child is a relevant data subject and the system does not provide transparent indicators or access notifications for parental review events.

title: Secondary use of child history for parental oversight may exceed the child's expectations
description: Historical data originally collected during the child's use of the service may later be used in a different context—parental oversight or evaluation. If this downstream use is not aligned with the original context understood by the child or not properly constrained, the flow creates an unawareness risk regarding how the child's data is used.
assumptions: Assumes the child interacts with the service directly and may not fully understand or expect retrospective parental review of all collected history.
uncertainty_note: Applicability depends on product context, age-appropriate notices, and whether parental review is clearly communicated at collection time.

description: Providing child history to the parent can raise non-compliance concerns if the system shares more data than necessary, lacks an appropriate legal basis or age-specific governance, or fails to provide required transparency and rights handling for the child as data subject. The privacy risk is located at this outbound flow because it operationalizes the disclosure.
assumptions: Assumes applicable child-privacy and general data-protection requirements impose purpose limitation, minimization, transparency, and access-control obligations on this disclosure.
